title: Princeton grows from the Big Spring at Eddy Grove
summary: Capt. William Prince found a big spring at Eddy Grove in 1797; Princeton grew around it and became the Caldwell County seat by 1817.
bodyMarkdown:
[Princeton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Princeton,_Kentucky) began at a spring. In 1797 a Revolutionary War captain named William Prince [explored a place called Eddy Grove](https://history.ky.gov/markers/william-prince-1752-1810), on the waters of Eddy Creek in western Kentucky. He found a large spring and good land around it, and the next year he brought his family to stay.

Prince had come a long way to get there. Born in Virginia in 1752, he moved with his family to Spartanburg County, South Carolina, in 1768, and during the Revolution he was a captain in Col. Benjamin Roebuck’s Spartan regiment. After the war he led a party of family and friends through Cumberland Gap, and in 1782 they settled on the Red River in Tennessee. Eddy Grove was his second frontier.

## The spring and the traces

The spring was the reason for everything that followed. Buffalo had worn paths to it long before people did, and the [Saline, Eddy and Varmint traces](https://history.ky.gov/markers/converging-of-indian-trails) met at the Big Spring. Indians and then settlers used the same routes, and in time they became the roads that still run out of town toward the Ohio and the Cumberland rivers.

On a bluff above the water, on the 200-acre survey he made in 1798, Prince built [Shandy Hall](https://history.ky.gov/markers/shandy-hall-princeton), a two-story stone house. By 1805 Eddy Grove had a post office, and [Prince’s Town was established](https://history.ky.gov/markers/william-prince-1752-1810) that same year.

## A county seat

The legislature [cut Caldwell County from Livingston](https://grokipedia.com/page/Princeton,_Kentucky) on January 31, 1809. The new county counted 4,268 people in 1810, and the seat of its courts was still an open question when Prince died that year. His widow then gave 50 acres for public use, including the lot where the first courthouse was built.

In 1817 Princetown, as it was then called, became the seat of Caldwell County ahead of Eddyville, its rival on the Cumberland, and [the next year the name became Princeton](https://history.ky.gov/markers/shandy-hall-princeton). The town was incorporated on December 6, 1820. Thomas Frazier’s inn, built near the spring, gave travelers a bed where the old traces met.

Settlement here came at a cost to the people who had used the land before. In 1838, Cherokee detachments forced west on the [Trail of Tears](https://history.ky.gov/markers/trail-of-tears) camped at the Big Spring on the Varmint Trace road toward the Cumberland River. The forced march began in the Great Smoky Mountains, ended in Indian Territory, and cost the Cherokee Nation nearly a third of its people. The town that grew from Prince’s spring was a stopping place on that road too.

## Kentucky today

Big Spring Park, off East Washington Street in downtown Princeton, holds the spring, the Shandy Hall and trail markers, and the Trail of Tears Commemorative Park, a certified site on the [Trail of Tears National Historic Trail](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trail_of_Tears). Water still runs out from under the limestone ledge, through the spring that drew William Prince to Eddy Grove in 1797.

The map pin marks Big Spring Park, at the Shandy Hall marker.
